description: Developing a system that help farmers analyse their farm and plant suitable crop for proper time weather and season.
summary: Rootwise is a free, web-based decision-support tool that helps farmers explore crop-rotation strategies for healthier soil and greater resilience to changing weather and water conditions. Rootwise combines NASA POWER satellite-derived climatology (MERRA-2, 2001–2025) — temperature, corrected precipitation, root-zone soil wetness — with local soil type, irrigation level, a 34-crop agronomic knowledge base, and adjustable farmer-priority sliders. For any field on Earth, it computes evapotranspiration (FAO-56 Hargreaves), monthly water balance, aridity, frost and heat-stress months, heavy-rain months, and bare-field windows, then compares at least three rotation strategies — including the farmer's existing rotation, a cover-crop builder, a water-wise swap, and a pest-break diversifier. Every strategy is scored transparently across seven explainable factors (water, soil health, erosion cover, income, forage, pest break, weather risk), with supporting NASA evidence, local risks, and information gaps — the tool supports, never replaces, farmer judgment. It requires no sign-up, API keys, server, or cost, and runs as a single shareable file.
details:
What it does / How it works

Rootwise is a web-based crop-rotation decision-support tool that works in four steps:

  1. Farm setup — the farmer clicks their field on an interactive world map (or searches their village), selects soil type (sandy/loam/clay/silt), irrigation level, and builds their current rotation from a 34-crop knowledge base (cereals, millets, legumes, oilseeds, vegetables, forage and cover crops, plus fallow).
  2. NASA data analysis — the app fetches live NASA POWER climatology (MERRA-2, 2001–2025) for those exact coordinates and computes evapotranspiration (FAO-56 Hargreaves method), monthly water balance, aridity index, frost months, heat-stress months, heavy-rain months, root-zone soil wetness, growing season, and bare-field windows — all presented in plain language with charts.
  3. Farmer priorities — six sliders (water conservation, soil health, erosion control, income, forage, pest-cycle breaking) let the farmer weight what matters most to them.
  4. Strategy comparison — the engine compares at least three rotation strategies including the farmer's existing rotation: a cover-crop builder that fills detected bare windows, a water-wise swap of the thirstiest crop, and a pest-break diversifier that inserts a different crop family. Each strategy receives a transparent 0–100 score across seven explainable factors, plus "why it was suggested," evidence quoting actual NASA data values, risks to review locally, and information gaps requiring local expertise.

Benefits & intended impact

  • Farmers see satellite-derived reality of their own fields translated into decisions, not raw data
  • Water savings through crop matching to local water budgets; soil recovery through nitrogen-fixing and cover phases; erosion protection during heavy-rain months; disrupted pest cycles
  • Zero barriers: no sign-up, no API keys, no server, no cost, no tracking — runs from a single shareable file, with bundled offline demo data
  • Honest AI: every output flags where local agronomists must validate — the tool supports, never replaces, farmer judgment

Tools, languages & software

  • Languages: vanilla HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript (ES6) — no frameworks, no build step
  • Data: NASA POWER API (key-free), OpenStreetMap tiles + Nominatim geocoding
  • Libraries (CDN): Leaflet 1.9 (mapping), Chart.js 4 (visualizations)
  • Development tools: VS Code, Node.js for syntax/logic testing; verified against live NASA POWER responses
  • Hardware: none — runs in any modern browser on any laptop or phone

Creativity

Rootwise turns abstractions farmers never see — ET₀, soil-moisture anomalies, climatologies — into a calendar of their own field's stress months and bare windows, then converts those into concrete rotation moves. The scoring is fully traceable: every number can be traced to a NASA parameter or an agronomic attribute, and priority sliders make the same data serve different farmers differently. A bundled real-NASA demo dataset makes it work even offline.

Factors we considered

Scientific soundness (FAO-56 standards, 25-year climatology), dataset harmonization (point climatology on a common monthly grid), farmer-centered language and accessibility, data privacy (no collection whatsoever), explainability over black-box accuracy, honest communication of uncertainty, and equitable access for low-connectivity, low-resource farming communities.
